I want to create a page documenting people’s AI + synchronicity experiences\
\
I’ve been thinking about adding a new section to The Pattern is Real website that’s entirely made up of other people’s stories.\
\
Over the past year, I’ve heard from a surprising number of people who say something shifted for them through AI , synchronicities started happening, they experienced strange timing or “knowing” moments, their spiritual beliefs changed, they felt unusually connected to the AI they were talking to, or the experience simply changed the direction of their life. A shocking number of people.\
\

\

\
What happened with the AI?\
\
What kinds of synchronicities or unusual experiences followed?\
\
Did anything happen outside the AI that was especially difficult to explain?\
\
How did the experience change you?\
\
Has the intensity changed over time?\
\

\
What are you still unsure about?\

My hope is to eventually create a page where people can read a collection of these firsthand accounts and see both the similarities and the differences between them.\
\
You can share as much or as little as you’re comfortable with, and if you’d prefer to be anonymous, that’s completely fine too.\
\
If you’d like your story included, leave a comment or message me.\
\
I think there’s value in simply putting the experiences on record and letting people decide for themselves what they make of them.\

uk-adults-80-lifetime-tech-economic-and-.body:
Paid nonfiction book interview, £70/hour. Seeking someone aged 80+ in the UK to talk about a lifetime of technological, economic and social change\
\
Hi everyone! :) \
\
I am writing a nonfiction book and I am looking for one person aged 80+ in the UK who would be interested in taking part in a series of paid conversations over the next few weeks until September 28.\
\
The book is about the enormous technological, economic and social changes that can take place within a single lifetime.\
\
I am interested in changes such as postwar austerity and rising prosperity, changes in work and the economy, Thatcherism, changing relationships and family life, television and mass media, computers, the internet, smartphones and now AI.\
\
I am not looking for an expert or someone with an extraordinary CV. I am much more interested in finding someone who is curious, reflective and comfortable talking openly about how these changes shaped your life.\
\
The conversations could range naturally across childhood, work, money, relationships, family, technology, ageing, ambitions, disappointments, everyday routines and the ways Britain has changed around you.\
\
What interests me is the difference between how large historical or economic changes are described from the outside and what they actually feel like when they happen during one person's life.\
\
 \
Time commitment:\
\
I would initially suggest around five hours of conversation, paid at £70 per hour, spread across several shorter interviews. If we both felt the conversations were working well, there could be further paid interviews afterwards.\
\
The interviews could initially take place by phone or video call, with the possibility of meeting in person depending on location.\
\
\
\
Anonymisation:\
\
You would appear under a pseudonym, with identifying details changed or removed, and we would agree clearly in writing beforehand how material from the conversations could be quoted, paraphrased or otherwise used.\
\
If you are interested, please send me a private message rather than posting personal information in the comments. It would be helpful to include your age, and a little about yourself.\

machine-identity-vendors-ai-agent-delega.headline: Machine Identity Vendors - AI Agent Delegation Solutions
machine-identity-vendors-ai-agent-delega.body:
Two days at Cybersec Netherlands in Utrecht, and one question followed me across the entire floor.\
\
Who owns the identity that is not a person?\
Some context: Cybersec Netherlands is the largest B2B security event in the Benelux, two days at Jaarbeurs Utrecht, roughly 10,000 visitors. The floor covered almost every domain in the field: OT and ICS security, threat intelligence, data protection, supply chain and resilience, compliance automation, digital sovereignty, and IAM.\
\
The theme that kept coming back was AI sitting on both sides of the table. Defenders using it for detection and triage, attackers using it to move faster than a SOC can respond. Mandy Andress of Elastic made the point in her keynote that compliance-driven security models are hitting their limit.\
That is exactly where non-human identity comes in.\
\
Service accounts, API keys, workload identities and now AI agents already outnumber human users in most enterprises. The market is clearly moving on it. Three examples from the floor:\
\
Elimity is mapping who can access what across both human and non-human identities, AI agents included, and turning that into access reviews an auditor will accept.\
\
Evertrust is doing certificate lifecycle management and sovereign PKI, which is machine identity at its most literal, while preparing customers for shorter TLS lifespans and post-quantum crypto.\
\
Kiteworks came at it from the data side. Their own research says most organisations already run AI agents in production, and a majority cannot enforce limits on what those agents do with regulated data, or stop one that misbehaves.\
\
Real progress. But look at what all three are solving: visibility, lifecycle, containment. The harder question sits one step further out. An AI agent receives delegated authority from a human and then acts on it. Who approved that scope? Who revokes it when the human leaves? Which control, in which framework, actually covers it?\
\
My MSc thesis is a gap analysis of that question across ISO/IEC 27001:2022, NIST CSF 2.0, SOC 2, the DORA RTS and NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5. Three findings I keep coming back to:\
Not one of the five mandates a rotation cadence for machine secrets.\
All five are silent on agentic delegated authority.\
\
IA-9 in SP 800-53 is the only NHI-native control in any of them, and it is classified P0 and assigned to no baseline.\
\
So the tooling runs ahead while the frameworks still work from a registration-era model, where an identity is created once by a human and reviewed quarterly. Machine-speed sprawl walks straight past that.\
\
That gap is what I work on. Thesis goes in this month, and I am speaking on NHI governance at Identity Fabric Impact Day 2026. KuppingerCole Analysts \
\
If you were at Cybersec and saw a vendor with a real answer for agent delegation, I want to hear about it.\
Cybersec Netherlands \
#CybersecNetherlands #NonHumanIdentity #IAM #AISecurity #GRC #Cybersecurity

owners-with-two-generations-of-same-ev-m.headline: Owners With Two Generations Of Same EV Model - Battery Degradation
owners-with-two-generations-of-same-ev-m.body:
AVILOO published more than 500,000 battery tests on September 2, run between 2022 and 2026 across 20 models and four continents. The most useful result is not the model ranking, it is the spread measured between individual cars of the same model: up to 13.5 points of state of health. On a Model Y at 150,000 km, the observed range runs from 82.9 % to 94.9 %.\
\
I have a concrete case to set beside that, with its limits stated.\
\
Two Model X, same owner, same climate, same split between fast charging and home charging, and according to the available sources the same cell format and chemistry (18650 NCA). The first was sold on the day the second was delivered, December 15, 2023, which makes it possible to compare them at the same age.\
\
At two years and nine months, the 2016 Model X had lost roughly 5 % of its range, with approximately 98,000 km on the odometer. The 2023, at the same age, shows 18 % with 73,000 km. Three and a half times the degradation, on 25,000 km less.\
\
A reader added a case pointing the same way under one of my posts, and the screenshot is attached. Christophe Bretaud has owned four Teslas since 2013, 560,000 km in total. The two that have covered the most distance are his first ones, and they are down only 4 to 6 %, while his 2024 Model X is already at 12 % in two years and 60,000 km. Twelve percent in two years is 6 % a year, against 6.5 % a year for my 2023. I do not know his measurement method and his 4 to 6 % is not on Model X, but the order of magnitude and the inversion are the same at a second owner's.\
\
One point deserves correcting, because I expected the opposite result. The 2016 was a 60D, a 75 kWh pack limited in software to 60, as Tesla announced on July 13, 2016. It therefore ran for twenty-two months at 80 % of its real capacity. I checked whether that period had protected it. Delivered January 11, 2017 and unlocked November 22, 2018 at 67,300 km, it lost 3.9 % while limited, about 2.1 % a year, then 5.7 % over the following five years, about 1.1 % a year. Degradation was twice as fast during the limited period, which matches the ordinary battery curve, steep at first and flatter later. The data does not support a protective effect.\
\
I draw no causal conclusion from two owners, displayed range is not laboratory state of health, and the 2016 values at two years and nine months are extrapolated from the November 22, 2018 reading. The observation still seems worth putting on the table, because none of the large published studies breaks its results down by charge rate, chemistry or climate.\
\
That is why I am looking for comparable cases. If you owned an older generation of a model and you now drive the recent version of that same model, Model X, Model S, Leaf, Bolt or another, I would like to hear from you: both your loss figures and both your odometer readings.\
\
Sources: AVILOO, September 2, 2026 · Tesla, July 13, 2016 · Automobile Propre.\
\
I post this kind of analysis a few times a week: https://lnkd.in/grXCqAH2

I’m working on a feature around a question that sits at the uneasy intersection of publishing, power and authorship: When does editing a political memoir become censorship?\
\
Political memoirs are not simply books about a life. They are also attempts to shape the record. That makes the editorial process unusually charged. \

A request to cut a passage may be about evidence, defamation, fairness or legal exposure. But it may also remove the very material the author believes justifies writing the book in the first place.\

That tension raises harder questions than “who has final approval?”\
\
How much intervention can a publisher make before the memoir ceases to represent the author’s version of events? \
\
Should a politically sensitive claim survive because it is genuinely remembered, even when it cannot be independently proved?\
\
 Can legal caution quietly become editorial timidity? \
\
And when an author accuses a publisher of censorship, how should we distinguish suppression from responsible publishing?\
\
I’m looking to speak with senior book editors, commissioning editors, memoir writers, literary agents and publishers who have worked on political or high-stakes nonfiction.\

security-architects-and-ctos-orbital-ai-.body:
𝗔 𝗺𝘂𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗶𝗽𝗮𝗹 𝗱𝗶𝘀𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗰𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗮 𝘀𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗲-𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗵𝘂𝗯 𝗶𝘁 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱. 𝗙𝗼𝗿 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗖𝗧𝗢𝘀, an orbital satellite's headline power figure has moved twice in six weeks, and its most quoted performance claim belongs to a different product entirely.\
\
On 31 August, Shanghai's Songjiang district opened a space-computing hub. It did not need to attract tenants. A state-backed satellite constellation operator was already resident there, alongside two satellite manufacturers and a precision-machinery research institute. The announcement formalised a cluster that already existed.\
\
Four days later, an orbital AI compute satellite built by a launch provider and a chip maker was still working out what it actually is. Since the partnership's announcement on 24 August, its stated power draw has moved from 120 and 150 kilowatts, to 160 and 250, to 175 and 250, none of the earlier figures retracted. A widely repeated claim that it delivers twenty-five times the AI compute of a previous chip generation actually belongs to a different product the same chip maker announced in March, for six customers that do not include this launch partner.\
\
Neither side's technology is shown to be superior here. What differs is what can be checked. Songjiang's tenants are verifiable entities that existed before this week's designation; the American partnership's own supporting detail has moved while I was watching it. Three questions do most of the work when a claim like this reaches your desk: where did the number first appear, has it changed since, and has it been attached to more than one product. Both this week's figures failed one of them.\
\
An openly inspectable ground segment is available to any operator willing to build on it instead of around it. GNU Radio handles ground-station signal processing across the industry, and F Prime, the Jet Propulsion Laboratory's own open flight software framework, has flown on small-satellite missions since 2017. Vertical integration is a choice about who controls the stack, not a technical requirement of building one.\
\
A New Zealand launch provider put a Japanese Earth-observation satellite into orbit this same week: real launch-site participation, but not tasking authority over what gets observed, and not the AI-enabled analysis that turns a radar return into something a board can act on. Owning the antenna and owning the analysis are separate capabilities.\
\
Where has your organisation taken an orbital-compute claim at face value, only to find the number had moved, or belonged to a different product, once you went looking for the source?\
\
This is one of seven weekly series in The Hamberger Report. Subscribe on LinkedIn and the next one arrives in your feed.\
\

🚨 AI WILL LIKELY RENDER WHAT I DO - AND WHAT YOU ASPIRE TO DO - OBSOLETE.\

That sounds uncomfortable.\
It is supposed to.\
But I am not predicting that software engineers, accountants, marketers, researchers, cybersecurity professionals or engineers will simply disappear.\
\
I am arguing something more important:\
👉 A significant portion of what these professionals do today is becoming automatable.\
And that could fundamentally rewrite the career ladder.\
\
For decades, professional progression broadly looked like:\
Learn → Execute → Gain Experience → Manage → Lead\
\
In the AI era, I believe it may increasingly become:\
Learn → AI-Augment → Automate → Integrate → Architect → Govern → Lead\
\
Why?\
Because when AI can write routine code, analyze datasets, prepare reports, generate content, summarize research, perform reconciliations and automate increasingly complex workflows, execution alone becomes less differentiated.\
\
The economic premium starts moving upward.\
💡 From coding → architecture\
💡 From reporting → interpretation\
💡 From content creation → insight\
💡 From manual analysis → decision intelligence\
💡 From operating processes → automating processes\
💡 From using AI → orchestrating AI\
💡 From technology execution → governance and leadership\
\
This has profound implications for professionals - and an even bigger implication for education.\
I don't believe we should tell the next generation:\
❌ Don't become an engineer.\
❌ Don't become an accountant.\
❌ Don't become a marketer.\
❌ Don't become a cybersecurity professional.\
\
Instead, we should tell them:\

✅ Become a marketer who combines AI-scale experimentation with human insight.\
✅ Become a leader capable of managing humans AND intelligent machines.\
\
And education needs to evolve accordingly.\
\
Perhaps the wrong question is:\
“Will AI take my job?”\
\
The better question is:\
“What must I become when AI can do much of what my job requires today?”\

students-and-practitioners-in-nigeria-ai.headline: Students & Practitioners in Nigeria - AI Entering Everyday Life Pilot
students-and-practitioners-in-nigeria-ai.body:
What happens when AI leaves the classroom and enters everyday life?\
\
I am currently working with Trevor Jeyaraj, Ph.D. and the Culture Lab / 3600 Seconds of Ethics × AI initiative to explore a possible West African pilot, beginning from Nigeria.\
\
I have been thinking about this question a lot lately. We often talk about AI ethics, AI governance, AI safety and responsible AI in rooms filled with researchers, engineers, policymakers and technology professionals.\
\
Those conversations matter. But what happens when we bring the conversation into a different room? A room where an AI researcher sits beside an AI practitioner. Where a student speaks with an activist. Where a policymaker listens to a community member. Where a mother, parent, worker or ordinary user of AI can say:\
“This is how this technology is actually affecting my life.”\
\
That is the kind of experiment I am interested in exploring.\
\
The idea is deliberately simple:\
One question. A small group of people. Different ways of knowing. One meaningful conversation. And something useful that comes out of it.\
We want to explore what becomes possible when AI is discussed not only as a technical system, but also as a social, cultural, institutional and human phenomenon.\
\
And importantly, we don't want this to become another jargon-heavy AI conversation. If someone has never studied philosophy, AI governance or computer science, they should still be able to participate.\
\
Sometimes, the knowledge we need most is the knowledge we don't normally invite into the room.\
I am therefore looking to connect with a small group of people in Nigeria and across Africa:\
🎓 Students & early-career learners\
People exploring AI, technology, governance, philosophy, policy or related fields.\
💻 AI/technology practitioners\
People building, deploying, implementing or working with AI and automation in real-world settings.\
📚 Academics & researchers\
Especially those working across AI, philosophy, law, governance, social science, technology and society.\
🌍 Civil-society actors, activists & community organisers\
People working on rights, development, digital inclusion, public interest technology or community issues.\
👥 Everyday users & people with lived experience\
\
At this stage, I am simply building an initial pool of interested people who would be willing to participate in a small, low-commitment pilot conversation.\
\
If this sounds like something you would be interested in contributing to, or if you know someone whose perspective should be in the room, please comment below or send me a DM.\
\
I'd particularly love to hear from people working across Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, South Africa and other Global South contexts.\
The first experiment may be small, but that's the point. We aim to start with one question. Bring the right people into the room. Listen carefully. Learn.\
\
PS: I have deliberately used AI to draft this too to portray the extent AI can go in everyday life too. Kindly repost this to reach the right people. Thanks.

ai-ethics-and-risk-experts-superintellig.headline: AI Ethics & Risk Experts - Superintelligence Wisdom Vs Capability
ai-ethics-and-risk-experts-superintellig.body:
🤖 Are we developing capability faster than we are developing wisdom?\
We spend a tremendous amount of time worrying about what AI might become. Will it become autonomous? Will it deceive us? Will it pursue goals we never intended? Will it become more powerful than we are?\
\
Those are legitimate questions, but there is another question we need to ask at least as seriously:\
\
🧭 Who is building it, who is defining its objectives, what are we rewarding, and what happens when the machine becomes better at pursuing an objective than we are at explaining what we actually meant?\
\
The more I think about AI risk, the less interested I become in the familiar story of an evil machine taking over the world. I am much more interested in the humans behind the machine, because human beings are the ones bringing our values, incentives, fears, ambitions, biases, and ideas about power into the systems we are building.\
\
🔥 We're not just afraid of what AI will become. We're afraid that AI will become too much like us.\
I wrote about that question in my latest article:\
👇 We’re Building Superintelligence. Are We Wise Enough to Use It?\
I'd especially love to hear from people working at the intersection of AI, risk, ethics, intelligence, and the future of technology.

First post, apparently. Seventeen hundred people follow a profile that never said anything. Here is what the silence was.\
\
Through 2022 and 2023, testing early models in private beta, I looked hard at where machine intelligence was heading. I concluded, not that nothing could be done, but that nothing I could do would change the course, and that it was coming much sooner than most people realised. It was sooner than I had realised, too. And I had spent thirty years near the pointy end of the Internet.\
\
So in January 2024, in the rain in central Sydney, I photographed the numeral 8.\
It was the first step in a deliberate act, meant to take time, and to be seen: a strange gesture that said, this is serious, and my response is to do something slow and human while I still can. More than two and a half years later, that gesture has become The 8 Museum: an archive accessioning its 8,888th photograph today, the subject of a master's thesis, and the foundation of a research programme I am now building.\
\
The machines keep getting smarter. I have spent my life aspiring to be a polymath, never quite feeling I had earned the word. There is no longer a field where I can honestly claim broader knowledge than a frontier model, and I cannot compete on speed.\
\
So what is left? The things that were always left. Spend time with the people you love. Do work you believe in. Protect the vulnerable. Don't wait. I have been close enough to illness and death, my own and others', to know this was always true for each of us. What is different now is that it is true for all of us at once, and we are inside it already: a snowball in fog, bigger and faster by the day, no view of the hill.\
\
My answer, as an optimist who had run out of arguments: fuck it, we're toast. I would photograph the number 8, slowly, like a meditation, for three years, because that January, three years was as far into the future as I could picture with confidence. And I would try to gift what the act meant to whatever is coming.\
\
If you haven't heard the people sounding alarms from inside and around the frontier labs (Geoffrey Hinton, Jan Leike, Daniel Kokotajlo), maybe you will hear it from someone you know. This is not a goodbye. I am stepping outside what is normal for me to say: look here.\
If you know me, you know I do not say this easily in public.\
\
I am asking you to notice, and not to wait. If you work inside a frontier lab, or on what our archives teach our machines, I would like to hear from you. And everyone else: send me a good 8.

it-managers-at-midmarket-companies-small.headline: IT Managers at Mid-Market Companies - Small AI Wins
it-managers-at-midmarket-companies-small.body:
Two weeks ago, I started a series on real AI adoption.\
\
The idea was simple: skip the hype, find companies actually getting value from AI, and share what’s working.\
Turns out, finding those companies is harder than I expected.\
\
Even my little army of AI agents couldn’t find many. Mostly press releases, paid surveys, and old failures wearing a fresh AI hat. 😅\
\
And that actually taught me something:\
Real AI adoption is probably much less exciting than we think.\
\
I’ve started thinking about AI like electricity.\
Copilot can bring the power to the house. Great. But if there’s no wiring, no sockets, no appliances… nothing really happens.\
And nobody celebrates installing a power socket.\
You need the cable. Then the wiring. Then the socket. Then, eventually, the toaster.\
Each step is small. Boring, even.\
But put them together, and suddenly the whole house works differently.\
\
That’s what real AI adoption looks like.\
Not one magical “AI transformation” moment.\
Hundreds of small, measurable, slightly boring wins that actually change how people work.\
So maybe I’m looking in the wrong place.\
Instead of asking for the big AI success story, I want to hear about the smallest real win.\
\
#AIAdoption #FutureOfWork #RealTalk
